After the work becomes easy
7 minutes by Arjun Shah

AI now does hard work in seconds, but something feels missing. Work used to shape the worker as much as it shaped the result. When a machine skips the struggle, we get the output but not the growth that came from making it. The real challenge now is choosing what deserves our effort and staying responsible for that choice.

Learn how leading teams are building and scaling AI agents in production
sponsored by LangChain

Agents can write and run code seconds before execution, often without human review. Local environments and standard containers weren’t designed for that level of autonomy. LangChain’s latest guide explains what safe agent execution requires, including isolation, permissions, observability, fast provisioning, and persistent state. Read the guide to learn when a managed sandbox makes sense, what capabilities to look for, and how to give agents the tools they need without handing them your infrastructure.

The work they can’t see
11 minutes by Christos Chatzis

Good engineering tends to become invisible because success quietly turns into expectation. A platform meeting revealed this clearly: an external expert recognized years of thoughtful decisions within an hour, yet internal leadership still had doubts. The gap was not technical understanding but missing context. Building great systems is only half the job. Making the reasoning behind them visible to decision makers is the other half.

AI adoption is a myth
10 minutes by Vas M.

Most employees who get access to AI tools barely use them, and those who do often use them poorly. Across large rollouts, about 10% of people drive nearly all real usage and value, while the rest see little to no impact. Tracking adoption as a yes or no metric hides this completely. The fix is to surface your power users, share what they build, and for everyone else, embed AI quietly into the systems they already use daily.

Beyond basic delegation: A group of leaders
6 minutes by Roman Nikolaev

Managers who try to handle everything themselves become bottlenecks, leaving their teams stuck and themselves burned out. Delegation works best in levels, from simple task handoff to full ownership of an outcome or area, and the goal is to push everyone toward that top level regardless of seniority. The short-term cost of mistakes and slipping timelines pays off as people grow. A team where everyone owns something is a team of leaders, not followers.

When you’re tapped out but still have to lead
6 minutes by Alex Ponomarev

Tiredness is normal in leadership, but there is a deeper level where pushing through causes real damage instead of growth. When you hit that point, cut your workload, respect your natural pace, and rest before a small problem becomes a long burnout. Your team watches how you handle your own limits, so modeling sustainable habits matters as much as any decision you make.
